title: Mixing a cone 6 clear liner glaze
subtitle: Weighing and mixing a lead-free cone 6 clear liner glaze from raw materials for a food-safe, glossy interior finish on stoneware
excerpt: A clear liner glaze is the most fundamental glaze in a functional pottery studio. Applied to the interior of mugs, bowls, and storage vessels, it seals the clay body and produces a smooth, food-safe surface under a clear gloss. This tutorial covers weighing, mixing, and sieving a standard cone 6 clear liner recipe from raw glaze chemicals, using a dry batch calculation and a simple jar-mill or hand mixing method.
sourceNotes: Cone 6 clear liner glaze recipe derived from the Leach standard clear base documented in Emmanuel Cooper, The Potter's Book of Glaze Recipes (2004, University of Pennsylvania Press) and adapted to lead-free cone 6 formulation. Mixing methodology from first principles.

glossaryTerms.definition: A glaze applied specifically to the interior of functional pottery to seal the clay body and provide a food-safe surface; clear liner glazes allow the clay body colour to show beneath
Silicon dioxide, the main glass-forming component in ceramic glazes; it raises the melting point and produces the glossy surface
A group of naturally occurring minerals that act as the main flux in cone 6 glazes, lowering the melting temperature of the silica
Pure white clay (China clay) added to glaze recipes in small amounts to suspend the glaze in water and add alumina to the melt

The ratio of the density of the glaze slop to the density of water; used to check that the glaze is mixed to the correct water-to-dry-material ratio. A cone 6 liner glaze typically fires well at a specific gravity of 1.40 to 1.45.

content.text: A cone 6 clear
liner glaze

uses four or five raw materials. Weigh them by dry batch weight. Mix with water to form a slop. Sieve to remove clumps before use. The recipe is simple. The discipline is in accurate weighing and careful sieving. These two steps determine whether the final glaze is smooth or gritty.

This is an advanced project. Raw glaze chemicals need careful handling. Weigh them accurately in grams. Check the specific gravity of the mixed glaze before firing. This confirms it is at the right consistency. A liner glaze mixed incorrectly can crawl, pinhole, or fail to mature. This ruins the work it was applied to.

attrs.title: Studio safety
attrs.content: Silica dust is the chronic studio hazard. Silicosis is irreversible. Mix wet whenever possible. Wear a P100 respirator any time raw glaze powders are open. Wet-clean only: no sweeping, no compressed air, no dry sanding indoors. Ventilation matters: a downdraft vent or open window with an extractor. Wear welder's shade-5 glasses when peephole-watching at high temperatures. Never open a hot kiln below 80 degrees Celsius. Keep a Class A fire extinguisher within reach. Handle raw oxides with gloves and a respirator. Never near food prep. All mixing work done wet, respirator on from the moment any dry powder container is opened.

content.text: When to use this technique

A correctly mixed liner glaze coats a bisque tile with an even, opaque white layer when dipped. After a cone 6 firing at 1220°C, the glaze should be smooth, clear, and glossy. There should be no pinholes, crawling, or bare patches. On buff stoneware, the clay colour shows through the glaze. On white stoneware or porcelain, the result is a near-clear finish.
What you need
Raw glaze materials for a standard cone 6 clear liner recipe (percentages of dry batch total, for a 1000 g test batch):
feldspar
(potassium or sodium type) 25 percent (250 g). Whiting (calcium carbonate) 20 percent (200 g).
Silica
325 mesh 35 percent (350 g).
Kaolin

10 percent (100 g). Zinc oxide 10 percent (100 g). Total dry batch weight 1000 g, yielding approximately 1.5 litres of mixed glaze slop at the correct specific gravity. You will also need: a kitchen scale accurate to 1 g, a large plastic bucket with a lid, water, a hand-held drill with a paint-mixing paddle or a long spoon for mixing, an 80-mesh glaze sieve, a second bucket to sieve into, a hydrometer for testing specific gravity, and nitrile gloves and a P100 respirator throughout.
Mixing the glaze: step by step
Set up in a ventilated area. Put on gloves and a P100 respirator before opening any powder containers. Lay all containers and tools on a damp cloth to contain any spilled powder.

Tare the scale to zero with the empty bucket on it. Weigh each dry ingredient directly into the bucket in order: feldspar first, then whiting, silica, kaolin, and zinc oxide. Weigh each to within 1 g of the target. Record the actual weights used.

Add approximately 600 ml of water to the dry materials. Do not add all the water at once: start with about half and mix thoroughly before adding more. The water should be added to the dry materials, not the other way around, to avoid raising a dust cloud from the dry powders.

Mix vigorously with the paddle or spoon for 3 to 4 minutes until no dry material remains at the base of the bucket. The mixture should look like smooth, thick cream. Add water gradually until the slop flows easily but is not watery.
Test the
specific gravity

: lower the hydrometer into the glaze slop and read the value at the liquid surface. A cone 6 clear liner glaze for brushing or dipping should read 1.40 to 1.45. Below 1.35 the glaze is too thin and will dry on the piece too quickly, giving a thin coat. Above 1.50 the glaze is too thick and may crawl during firing. Adjust by adding water to lower specific gravity, or leaving the bucket uncovered for an hour to evaporate moisture and raise it.

Sieve the mixed glaze through an 80-mesh glaze sieve into the clean second bucket. Pour the glaze through the sieve steadily and use a rubber spatula to push any material through that catches on the mesh. Pass the glaze through the sieve twice for a smooth result. Discard anything that will not pass through the sieve after a firm second push.

Label the bucket clearly with the recipe name, batch date, specific gravity, and cone target. Store covered to prevent dust contamination and evaporation. Stir thoroughly before each use: liner glazes settle on standing.
What it looks like when it's right

A correctly mixed liner glaze coats a bisque tile with an even, opaque white layer when dipped. After a cone 6 firing at 1220°C, the glaze should be smooth, clear, and glossy. There should be no pinholes, crawling, or bare patches. On buff stoneware, the clay colour shows through the glaze. On white stoneware or porcelain, the result is a near-clear finish.
Always fire a test tile from each new batch before glazing production work. A test tile from the same clay body and bisque schedule as your pieces gives a reliable preview of the fired result.
Common mistakes

Not wearing a respirator when handling dry powders. Silica and feldspar in dry form are silica dust hazards. Mix wet and wear a P100 respirator from the moment any dry container is opened until all powder is fully wetted and mixed.
Skipping the specific gravity test. A glaze mixed by eye without measurement will be inconsistent between batches. Test every fresh batch with the hydrometer and adjust before applying to work.

Using a different feldspar to the recipe without adjustment. Potassium feldspar and sodium feldspar behave differently at cone 6. If you substitute one for the other the glaze will mature at a slightly different temperature and the surface quality will change. Test any substitution on a tile before using on production pieces.

Skipping the second sieve pass. Glaze materials contain lumps, particularly whiting and zinc oxide, that will not fully dissolve in one pass through the sieve. Unsieved lumps fire as white specks or crawling patches on the glaze surface.

Not applying to a test tile first. Even a known recipe can behave differently on a new clay body, at a different kiln position, or with a different bisque schedule. One test tile before a full production glaze firing is the minimum due diligence for any new batch.
